item.title: Thieves Smash Museum Case for Diamond Necklace Worth Millions in Vienna
item.description:
In a brazen robbery, two men stole a diamond necklace once owned by an Egyptian queen from a museum in Vienna, the Austrian police said, adding that they were searching for the thieves.

The men smashed a display case and took the necklace on Thursday afternoon, the police said in a statement, and they then “fled with the jewelry in an unknown direction.”

The Museum of Applied Arts, where the theft occurred, said in a statement that the item was taken from an exhibition of works by the French luxury jeweler Van Cleef & Arpels.

One of the thieves was armed, the museum said, although it did not specify with what, and no one was harmed. The museum’s surveillance system recorded the thieves, museum officials said, and the police described the robbers as two slim men with dark hair and short beards.

The platinum-and-diamond necklace, which dates to at least 1939, was once owned by Queen Nazli, the second wife of King Fouad of Egypt. She was stripped of her royal status in 1950 by her son, King Farouk, because she supported her daughter’s secret marriage in San Francisco to a Coptic Christian diplomat. By then, she and her daughter were living in the United States.

A military coup overthrew King Farouk in 1952, and a year later Egypt’s new authorities seized the former royal family’s property. (The deposed king died in 1965, aged 45, after collapsing at a restaurant north of Rome, where he was living in exile.)

The former queen and her daughter lived first in mansions in Beverly Hills and Hawaii and then in an apartment in West Los Angeles. They were trailed by debt, and in 1976 the former queen’s jewels were put up for sale in a Los Angeles bankruptcy court. Nazli died in Beverly Hills two years later, at 83.

The necklace, part of an exhibit scheduled to run through September, wound up among the holdings of the auction house Sotheby’s, which in 2015 estimated it was worth between $3.6 million and $4.6 million.

“The theft of a high-value piece of jewelry by Van Cleef & Arpels has hit us hard,” the museum’s general director, Lilli Hollein, said in a statement. “Especially considering the incidents at major museums in recent years, we took this as an opportunity to thoroughly review our own security measures at the museum in general.”

Thieves have targeted several high-profile European museums since last fall, stealing jewels during an extraordinary heist at the Louvre in Paris, paintings by Renoir, Cézanne, Matisse, and Antonello da Messina from museums in Italy and gold and silver Bronze Age objects from a museum in Spain.

“Even with comprehensive security measures in place, a targeted, armed attack during ongoing exhibition operations cannot be completely ruled out,” Ms. Hollein said.

item.title: ‘A New Form of U.S. Colonialism’: Venezuelans Bristle at U.S. Oil Takeover
item.description:
Many Venezuelans suspected that there was going to be a price to pay for President Trump’s brazen capture of their autocratic leader, Nicolás Maduro, who was arrested by U.S. forces in January.

On Friday, that cost became clear when Mr. Trump announced that the U.S. would be taking majority control of a vast part of Venezuela’s oil reserves — national resources long considered by many in the country to be a birthright.

By Saturday, many Venezuelans were grappling with whether they were willing to pay that price. So far, the U.S. ouster of the autocrat has done little to change the country — Mr. Maduro’s successor, Delcy Rodríguez, remains in power, while millions of everyday Venezuelans remain in poverty, electricity blackouts continue to plague the nation and no date has been set for an election.

The new deal could bring major investment. But many Venezuelans want overall economic and political change. The accord guarantees neither and could deepen the relationship between Mr. Trump and Ms. Rodríguez, further entrenching her in power.

In Valencia, about two hours from the capital of Caracas, José Leal, 68, a retired educator, said the $100 billion in promised U.S. investment sounded small compared to the 65 billion barrels Venezuela was giving up. But after decades under a repressive government, he was willing to put up with this deal — and hope that Mr. Trump would push for democratic change.

“Obviously, the United States comes out ahead, enormously so,” he said. But “the Americans hold the power,” he said, and without them “we won’t manage to break free from the socialism of Chávez and Maduro. Without them, we’ll remain trapped like Cuba, China, or North Korea.”

“It’s not that I love it or even like it,” he said of the deal. “I consider it a necessary evil. If we manage to escape this entire disaster — which we’ve endured for 27 years and the Cubans for 68 — if we manage to get out of this mess, then even though I don’t like it, it will be worth it.”

Others were not so optimistic. The Venezuelan government has a long history of doling out beneficial contracts to the wealthy and connected, known inside the country as “enchufado” — people who are “plugged in” — while everyday Venezuelans suffer. Mr. Trump’s announcement on Friday included no mention of a democratic transition.

A meme began circulating in the region almost as soon as the deal was announced. “I want you to get rid of Chavismo,” says a cartoon Venezuelan man, referring to Mr. Maduro’s movement, “and leave us our oil.”

A cartoon Mr. Trump responds: “Take the oil and leave you with Chavismo, got it!”

Venezuela, home to some of the largest oil reserves in the world, nationalized those resources in the 1970s. Sovereign control over wells then became a core pillar of the ideology of the socialist government, founded by former president Hugo Chávez.

Ms. Rodríguez’s decision to turn over much of that oil to the U.S. government represented an astounding about-face, one that few Venezuelans could have imagined before the January attack.

That turnaround was evident in a statement released by Ms. Rodríguez’s Socialist Party on Saturday, which said that “true to its historic commitment to national sovereignty,” the party was extending its full support for the deal and the decisions made by “Comrade Delcy Rodríguez.”

The irony of this was not lost on many Venezuelans. A government that once proudly thumbed its nose at Washington was now handing over the resources at the center of its identity.

Another meme circulating in Venezuela changed the logo of the national oil company, PDVSA, to PDUSA.

On X, Rafael Ramírez, a Chávez loyalist and former head of PDVSA now living in exile, accused Ms. Rodríguez of “opening the doors to a new form of US colonialism.”

In Maracaibo, a Venezuelan city that anchors much of the country’s oil industry, Dario Nava, 67, a former PDVSA manager, said he opposed the deal and did not believe it would improve his life.

“The United States is going to manage our oil industry,” he said, “and sovereignty is lost there.”

In Caracas, Carlos Arenas, 24, a university student, said that he might be willing to cede some control of Venezuelan oil for economic improvement.

“If there were an economic benefit for the country that eventually translated into a better quality of life for Venezuelans, then yes, I would be willing,” he said. “But that doesn’t seem to be the case here — at least not initially.”

“Unfortunately, it doesn’t look like there will be a political change in Venezuela anytime soon,” he added. “Trump seems very comfortable with Delcy.”

Venezuela’s leading opposition figure, María Corina Machado, has in the past floated the idea of privatizing the oil sector. For years the idea was mocked by Ms. Rodríguez’s party. And it was so controversial that Ms. Machado did not make it a core part of her platform in a 2024 presidential election.

On Saturday, a prominent supporter of Ms. Machado, Walter Molina, said on X that “Venezuelans always knew that our freedom would come at a cost.”

“If that price is 65 billion barrels over the course of decades, so be it,” he said. “But let it be just that: the price of our freedom. Not the price we pay to keep a criminal tyranny in de facto power — only now kneeling before the United States.”

Reporting was contributed by María Victoria Fermín from Caracas, Tibisay Romero from Valencia, Venezuela, and Sheyla Urdaneta from Buenos Aires.

item.title: The 10 p.m. Dinner Is a Spanish Tradition. Are People Giving It Up?
item.description:
For generations, dinnertime for the Terrazas family, as in many households in Spain, was late. It usually began after 10 p.m. and often stretched past midnight.

But now, Antonio Terrazas, a tax adviser in Madrid, says his family sits down to eat around 9 p.m. When they dine out, they’re also eating earlier, and have noticed their friends are, too.

“At first it was strange. We’d look at each other like, ‘Madre mía, who would believe that we’d be seated at a restaurant and eating at 9 o’clock?” Mr. Terrazas said. “But not anymore.”

In Spain, known for its night-owl energy, a quiet revolution appears to be unfolding in one of its best known cultural institutions: the late-night dinner.

Spaniards have long eaten later than people elsewhere in Europe, a tradition that many see as part of the national identity. By custom, families gather around their dinner tables late at night and restaurants remain filled long past the time when much of the industrialized world has turned in.

Spain held fast to the practice even as experts debated whether it was a drag on the economy, producing a work force that was more tired and less productive than it could be.

But evidence suggests that Spain is moving dinnertime up.

CoverManager, an online platform that manages reservations for thousands of Spanish restaurants, reports that half the dinner bookings now are for before 9 p.m., compared with 27 percent a decade ago. TheFork, a similar platform, said its 8 p.m. bookings in Spain have nearly tripled from 2019, while 10 p.m. reservations have halved.

Around half of dinner reservations in Spain are now made for before 9 p.m.

Source: CoverManager/BigQuery.

Adina Renner/The New York Times

In Spanish homes, too, there are subtle signs of a shift. A government survey conducted in 2024 in the Catalonia region suggests that people there are starting their evening routines, including dinnertime, moderately earlier compared with 2010. National data are not yet available, so experts said it was too early to draw broader conclusions.

While the reasons for the change are not entirely clear, Marta Junqué Surià, the director of Time Use Initiative, a nonprofit based in Barcelona that advocates for policies around sleep and wellness, pointed to the pandemic, which ruptured old routines, and suggested more people were seeking the health benefits associated with earlier mealtimes.

“We are heading toward more biological rhythms that allow us to eat better and, above all, get better rest,” Ms. Junqué said.

Mr. Terrazas, 58, a father of two, said that he and his wife simply wanted better sleep.

“It’s been a positive change,” he said.

The New York Times asked CoverManager, which handles online bookings for about 16,000 Spanish restaurants, to analyze the roughly 330 million reservations it had recorded in the country over the past decade.

The data show a clear pattern, said Thomas Jeanjean, chief executive of Hospitality Tech Group, which owns CoverManager: “The late dinner is dying.”

The typical dinner out in Spain today begins an hour earlier than before the pandemic, according to the data.

Later reservations are increasingly rare: 10 p.m. seatings made up 15 percent of dinner bookings last year, down from 30 percent in 2016. Tables for 11 p.m. accounted for 1.9 percent, compared with 5.7 percent in 2016.

“Dinner times have moved earlier,” Mr. Jeanjean said, “and the curve is still bending.”

The late dinner hasn’t disappeared: People typically eat an hour later on weekends and about 20 minutes later in the summer than in the winter, the data indicates, and 9 p.m. remains the most popular reservation time.

TheFork, which works with more than 12,000 restaurants in Spain, said that surging foreign tourism was one factor in the shift, though it noted that about 70 percent of its reservations come from Spanish phone numbers.

CoverManager said tourists weren’t driving the change, noting that users with Spanish numbers, who accounted for around 90 percent of its reservations, were booking tables for around an hour earlier than a decade ago.

Spanish society is transforming, having added more than a million foreign-born workers since 2018, many from Latin America. But in a country of 50 million people, the turn toward earlier dining is “a homegrown change of habit,” Mr. Jeanjean concluded.

Dining late is a relatively modern Spanish custom. During World War II, the dictator General Francisco Franco pushed clocks on the Spanish mainland forward an hour. Spain never reverted, meaning its official time runs ahead of its geographic position.

Late dining was also reinforced by the poverty of the postwar years, Ms. Junqué said, when many people worked two jobs, eating dinner only after their second shift. The Spanish workday, often punctuated by a long afternoon break, ends later than elsewhere in Europe.

The coronavirus pandemic, which prompted a nationwide 11 p.m. curfew in October 2020, encouraged people to dine out earlier and contributed to a revival of tardeo, the custom of eating, drinking and socializing in the late afternoon, according to bookings by CoverManager. Sometimes, experts say, Spaniards now replace dinner with tardeo.

More restaurant reservations are now made for between 5 and 7 p.m.

Source: CoverManager/BigQuery.

Adina Renner/The New York Times

After pandemic restrictions eased, many restaurants kept the earlier schedules to save on labor and operating costs, said José Luis Álvarez Almeida, the president of Hostelería de España, a business confederation representing the hospitality sector.

In conversations this summer, many Spaniards said they were eating earlier than in years past. All seemed to have their own reasons — age, young children, a desire for better health or more energy in the morning.

Nacho Calvo Vila, 53, a restaurant owner in Barcelona, said he made the change around five years ago to improve digestion and get better sleep. Now he goes to bed around 10 p.m., his old dinner time. Better rest has helped him make healthier decisions around his diet, temper his anxiety and regulate his emotions, he said.

“Sleep is fundamental,” he said. “I think it’s one of the biggest areas where mind-sets are changing, especially here in Spain.”

Out for drinks with colleagues in Madrid, Sol Fauquier, 46, said she now preferred to dine at 8 p.m. and suspects others want to eat earlier, too, but social pressure discourages people from being the first to suggest it.

“I don’t really face any resistance — quite the opposite,” she said. “I’ve found that when I suggest meeting early — say, at 8 or 8:30 — people never say no.”

Her colleague Isabel Cano, 23, interjected that dining so early was “unthinkable” and “not the Spanish spirit.”

If someone invited her to dinner at 6:30, Ms. Cano said she’d tell them to wait. “Like, just have a muffin.”

Experts argue that Spain could reap a host of benefits if people ate and went to bed earlier.

It would be “a more productive, healthier and happier country,” Ms. Junqué said. She cited studies showing that, in countries where people sleep more, “productivity increases and the mental health of the population is better.”

In 2013, a parliamentary commission found that Spaniards were getting about an hour less sleep than the European average, and linked worker fatigue to lower productivity and absences on the job.

But official measures to encourage earlier dinner times appear likely to face resistance. When Spain’s left-leaning labor minister, Yolanda Díaz, suggested in 2024 that a late-night culture that pushed restaurants to remain open past midnight was “madness,” Madrid’s conservative regional president, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, retorted that the national government preferred Spaniards to be “bored and at home.”

Ms. Junqué argued that even if late dining fades, what it means for Spaniards to sit at the table with family and friends would not.

“We love being around people and socializing,” she said. “Our Spanish culture is going to remain exactly what it is.”

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting from Madrid.

item.title: Deportees Recount Harrowing Journeys to Africa: Shackles, a ‘Freezer’ and Blows
item.description:
Leonardo Sánchez wailed in pain for hours on the deportation flight from Louisiana to West Africa, he and six other detainees said.

He’d been cuffed around his wrists and ankles. A chain around his waist dug into his grossly protruding abdomen — the result of years-old wounds and surgeries that doctors said left his intestines barely inside his body.

Mr. Sánchez, a 49-year-old Cuban, begged for medical attention from several of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on the aircraft.

“I was in pain, crying like a little kid,” he said. But the agents wouldn’t remove his chains or let him use the toilet, he and other detainees said. He wet himself.

Like many of the more than two dozen deportees on the flight with him, Mr. Sánchez said he did not know where he was being taken. Several panicked when they suspected it was Liberia, after one of them saw it written on a sheet of paper held by an ICE official in Louisiana.

AFRICA

mali

NIGERIA

ivory

coast

ghana

Monrovia

Marshall

liberia

Malabo

equatorial

guinea

Atlantic

Ocean

gabon

500 miles

The New York Times

When some protested, they were beaten by agents, five of the deportees said. Some were slammed to the ground or struck with blows, several said. One showed cuts along his wrists and bruises around his neck, which he said he received after resisting getting on the plane. Another said some deportees were left screaming in pain.

The planeload of deportees, which arrived in Liberia this month, carried the first of 1,200 people expected to be sent to the West African country by the United States over the next year. The arrangement is one of the largest in a growing number of deals the Trump administration has made to send deportees — including people with court orders protecting them from being sent back to their home countries — to nations halfway across the world where they have no ties.

In recent weeks, the White House has pushed to expand these so-called third-country deportation efforts and boost the number of people expelled from the United States, according to a U.S. official. In July, ICE arrests jumped to nearly 50,000 people, and the administration has focused on deporting people who have been able to remain in the country for years with court orders protecting them from being sent home, another official added.

The New York Times interviewed 10 of the deportees on the flight to Liberia, all of whom described a harrowing journey that included months in detention in the United States and a panicked 14-hour expulsion to Africa, in which agents wrestled and shackled frightened detainees.

Several spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals. All of them said they experienced or witnessed what they described as abusive or violent treatment by ICE officials during the course of their deportation or while in detention in the United States.

“They didn’t treat us like people, like human beings,” said Carlos Téllez-Sanchez, a deportee from Venezuela who was expelled to Liberia. “They can say or do anything to you and there’s nothing you can do.”

The White House, Department of Homeland Security and State Department said in statements that the only deportees being sent to third countries are those who cannot be returned to their home nations or refuse to go back.

“As Secretary Rubio has said, we remain unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration,” said Tommy Pigott, a State Department spokesman.

When the flight arrived in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, Mr. Sánchez, the Cuban national, and three others said they refused to disembark, afraid of being abandoned in an unfamiliar country. They said they were forced onto the tarmac by ICE officers who yanked and twisted their handcuffs, pinned them to the ground and pressed their knees directly onto their necks.

Mr. Sánchez said the federal agents knocked him onto the ground and knelt on his bulging abdomen, leaving him in agony, his pants still damp with urine. Other deportees began shouting, “‘You abuser! If he dies, it’s on you!’” Mr. Sánchez and three other deportees said.

The Department of Homeland Security said that no detainees were refused access to the bathroom, that Mr. Sánchez was reviewed and declared fit to fly by medical staff, that his medical needs were addressed on the flight, and that agents did not kneel or press on his abdomen.

It did not address the deportees’ other allegations of abuse.

Mr. Sánchez, crying in pain, said he was carried back onto the flight in Liberia with the others. Then, they were then taken to Equatorial Guinea, one of at least 35 countries with which the United States has struck deportation deals, most of them in Africa.

“Basically, they treated us like we were wild animals,” said Carlos Rodríguez, another Cuban national on the flight. “Like beasts.”

Three of the deportees, including 21-year-old Paola Dos Santos, a Brazilian national who was deported to Liberia, said they suffered “psychological torture” from ICE officials while detained in the United States.

Ms. Dos Santos, who said she was detained for 15 months in two separate U.S. facilities, recounted detainees routinely being denied medical care, including pregnant women. One woman who pleaded for information about her son, who had been separated from her, had her hands and ankles tied together, Ms. Dos Santos said: “They tied her like she was a cattle.”

The Department of Homeland Security said that detainees receive “comprehensive medical care” from the moment they enter ICE custody, including dental, mental health services and prenatal and postnatal care.

Some of the deportees said they were constantly moved from facility to facility, and sometimes kept in detention centers where up to 50 people shared a single toilet. Many said they were held for days in a painfully cold room without beds that they called “the freezer.”

Late last year, Mr. Téllez-Sanchez, the deportee from Venezuela, said he was working at a car dealership in Dallas and looking forward to the birth of his son. He’d been in the United States for five years after a judge granted him an order protecting him from being sent back to his home country, he and a lawyer working with him said. Then in December, he was arrested on a routine visit to renew his work permit.

When he tried to explain to immigration officials that he had a court order preventing his deportation, he said an ICE agent told him to shut up.

He said he witnessed constant verbal abuse by ICE officials while in detention. While parts of the deportees’ accounts could not be independently verified, The Times was able confirm certain details with lawyers and government officials.

“The whole time, I cooperated,” Mr. Téllez-Sanchez said. “I got a lawyer, I started a legal case. I didn’t want to risk it, I wanted to do the right thing.”

“They didn’t care,” he added.

In eight months of detention, he was moved more than six times, he said. Alma David, the lawyer working with him, said that constantly moving deportees between states was a common tactic by ICE to prevent detainees from launching legal challenges.

“It’s a kind of psychological warfare,” she said.

Deportees are often confused when they are arrested while trying to renew their work permits or asylum papers, unaware that ICE officials are targeting people who have protection orders like Mr. Téllez-Sanchez, said Ms. David.

The administration’s rapid deportations to third countries are being contested in the courts. In February, a judge declared the policy unlawful, but an appeals court has allowed the government to continue the deportations while it reviews the case.

Now, the Trump administration is boosting deportations by sending people “to countries like Liberia where they have zero ties, don’t speak the language and simply cannot imagine surviving,” said Ms. David.

Mr. Sánchez, the Cuban man who was writhing in pain on the flight to Liberia, said he had arrived in the United States in 2010 under the Cuban Adjustment Act and worked as a welder, building windows and doors.

In 2018, he was stabbed and shot in his stomach during a robbery in Miami that left him in a coma for 40 days, he said. Doctors who reviewed pictures of his abdomen said they appeared consistent with his descriptions of what happened to him.

In early 2025, he said he received a one-year probation order following a traffic stop that resulted in a conviction for cocaine possession. He said he completed 40 hours of community service and paid a $3,200 fine. The Department of Homeland Security said Mr. Sánchez was a criminal who “received due process and was ordered removed from the United States” in May.

When the flight landed in Liberia, deportees said ICE agents called their names one by one to exit the plane, and that those who resisted were forcibly removed. Mr. Rodríguez, one of the Cubans, said he had four officers on top of him at once.

Several deportees who resisted disembarking said they got back on the plane after being told they would be returned to the United States.

Instead, they were taken to Equatorial Guinea, loaded into a van, left at a hotel and barred from leaving. They are under constant watch by guards carrying automatic weapons, they said in phone interviews.

“They told us: ‘If you try to escape, we’re going to shoot off your feet,’” said Darwin Hernández, also from Cuba.

The doctors who reviewed pictures of Mr. Sánchez’s abdomen said his condition did not appear to be life threatening, but that the thin layer of grafted skin holding in his intestines was extremely vulnerable, susceptible to injury and should be repaired through surgery.

When he finally saw medical staff in Equatorial Guinea, Mr. Sánchez said, doctors there told him that the country lacked the equipment needed to treat him. They gave him a simple painkiller, he said.

In Liberia, where most of the deportees were taken, Mr. Téllez-Sanchez, the Venezuelan, is trying to make sense of his new surroundings.

He and a few others occasionally take short walks, leaving the partly built, three-story hotel they were placed in by the Liberian government. Outside, over half a dozen security guards and Liberian officials stand watch.

“They said we have freedom to move around, but I don’t feel free,” Mr. Téllez-Sanchez said. “I’m not a criminal. I don’t deserve what has happened to me.”

Liberia said that none of the deportees it has taken are criminals, and that they would be allowed to apply for residency in the country.

Officials from the International Organization for Migration, a U.N. agency, said in a statement that they had provided assistance to the deportees, and would help send them back to their home countries or find “other available pathways.”

Many of the deportees are now trying to figure out what to do — settle in an unfamiliar African nation or return to countries where they fear persecution?

Mr. Téllez-Sanchez, who fled Venezuela in 2019, said he hoped to be allowed back in the United States, but was not so optimistic: “Maybe it won’t be possible.”

For now, he said, he just wants to see his family, including the newborn son he has yet to hold.

Mattathias Schwartz contributed reporting.

item.title: Pilgrims to Flood-Stricken Nepal Sought the Divine at Sacred Mountain
item.description:
Many pilgrims to Mount Kailash, a sacred, snowcapped peak in the Himalayan region, only complete the trek once in their lifetime.

Making the trip to the remote mountainous region on the border of Nepal and Tibet can take months of planning, a small fortune and untold physical fortitude. The goal for those who make the journey is to take a step toward spiritual awakening on God’s doorstep.

When Amita Amin, 67, left her home in New York for Kailash this month, shepherding a small group of other local Hindu pilgrims, she was marking her seventh journey to the mountain — and her second trip this year.

“She believed in God so much,” said Aditi Patel, Ms. Amin’s daughter-in-law. “She just wanted to be close to his abode, as much as possible.”

Ms. Amin’s group was at the border on Wednesday morning, according to Dipak Lamicchane, who runs Trekking Planner Nepal, the tour company Ms. Amin uses on her trips. A flash flood triggered by glacial runoff ripped through the region about an hour after their last communication, he said from his home in Kathmandu, Nepal.

The group of pilgrims and their three Nepalese guides, including Mr. Lamicchane’s son-in-law, have not been heard from since.

Tens of thousands of tourists and pilgrims have already traveled to the area around Kailash this season, which runs from about May to September, Mr. Lamicchane said, because of colder weather during the rest of the year. Adventurers of all stripes visit the site, which regularly tops lists of the world’s best treks for its pristine natural beauty and rugged terrain.

The area is also sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs and those who follow the Bon tradition of Tibetan Buddhism. Visiting Kailash is not about conquering the mountain. It is about surrender, a belief that the journey itself draws pilgrims closer to the divine.

Hindus believe Mount Kailash is the home of Shiva, the god of destruction, transformation and meditation, and his wife, Parvati. The mountain is also an impressive topographical feature, a natural pyramid that slices 21,778 feet into blue Tibetan skies.

“It is generating an inner heat, Hindus would say,” said Dr. Steven Vose, a professor at the University of Colorado Denver who studies South Asian religious traditions. “That heat is transformative. It helps you step closer to enlightenment and liberation.”

A typical pilgrimage involves walking around the entirety of the mountain, about 33 miles, over several days. Snow melt from the mountain, which is believed to be so holy that attempts to summit its peak are banned, feeds Lake Manasarovar, also a holy site believed to be where Shiva bathes.

“If you’re auspicious enough,” said Dhruv Amin, Ms. Amin’s son, “you may even see him come down the mountain to bless you at night.”

Mr. Amin, 43, made the trip with his mother in 2010. He had already visited four sacred Hindu temples in India, and going to Kailash was a final pilgrimage before entering his medical residency. Trekking the mountain with his mother, he said, felt “as if God was watching us.”

“When I think of God,” Mr. Amin told The Times, “I think of the mountain.”

For Tibetan Buddhists, Mount Kailash is believed to be the dwelling place of a tantric deity, a place where pilgrims go to purify themselves, obtain blessings and advance their spiritual journey toward awakening.

Followers of Jainism, an Indian religion that aspires to spiritual purity and nonviolence, believe that their first spiritual teacher attained liberation by ascending the mountain. It is considered “the high-water mark of devotion, combined with yoga and asceticism,” Dr. Vose said.

In Sikhism, the mountain is said to be where the faith’s first guru undertook a famous dialogue with yogis of the Himalayas.

Kailash is “such a significant geographic and multi-faith landscape with spiritual potency,” said Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, a Sikh scholar and the chair of religious studies at Colby College in Maine. Ms. Singh’s mother’s name is Kailash.

Across all faiths, the journey to and around Mount Kailash was once only thought possible through mythical attainment. Even in the modern era, the trip remains arduous. Some pilgrims, particularly Tibetan Buddhists, enhance the already difficult journey by prostrating themselves the entire length of the trek.

“There is sacrifice involved,” said Dr. Jeffery D. Long, a professor of religion, philosophy and Asian studies at Elizabethtown College in Pennsylvania. “It adds to a sense of sanctity, humility, wearing down your ego.”

Ms. Amin did not anticipate making her latest pilgrimage to Kailash. But Tejal Patel, Ms. Patel's mother, had never made the journey and wanted to do so alongside family. About six months ago, the two women began planning. Ms. Patel, 64, started going to the gym.

A small group of other local Hindus decided to join them, preparing for the trip through video calls. Neelam and Ramesh Sharma, a couple from Queens, undertook the pilgrimage as part of their retirement. The pair, both in their 60s, have also not been heard from since the flood, their family said.

The risk involved in such a voyage was not lost on pilgrims like Ms. Amin. Before each trip, her son said, she would remark that it might be her last.

At least 675 deaths have been confirmed as a result of the catastrophic floods, and another 2,400 people were missing as of Saturday. More than 7,000 survivors have been rescued.

Mr. Amin wants to believe that his mother is stranded on the Chinese side of the border, where the bridge connecting China and Nepal has been destroyed and communication lines have been cut off. He hopes the group will be found, alive. That way, Ms. Amin can tell the tale of their miraculous survival, there at the door to God’s house.

item.title: See Nepali Rescue Workers Testing Aid Delivery by Drone
item.description:
The deadly flood and landslide that struck Nepal last week snapped bridges and roads and yanked out utility poles, abruptly cutting off transportation and communication for thousands.

As the search for more than 2,500 people continues, there’s also a rush to move food and other essentials to survivors on either side of the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli Rivers. There are about 10,000 households affected by the disaster, according to the United Nations.

One idea to deliver the aid: drones.

On Saturday afternoon, about a dozen private drone operators, army volunteers and police officers gathered on a patch of open ground in Devighat, an area in the central Nepali town of Bidur, to test whether the devices could be used to deliver critical supplies across the Trishuli River.

They were testing a drone that was roughly the size of a large dining table when its propellers were extended. It could carry up to 220 pounds.

Some of the testers were experienced commercial drone pilots who had dropped off packages high in the Himalayas. But the group trod cautiously, loading the drone with a payload of around 130 pounds before its first twirl in the sky.

The packages included rice, instant noodles, clothing and sanitary pads. Light rain slowed the work of attaching the goods to the drone with ropes and carabiners.

Drones of this size and capacity, which cost thousands of dollars, can climb thousands of feet, but the drone in the test flew much lower to the other side of the river. It did not land there but hovered as testers offloaded the goods. A round trip took about three minutes.

After its first successful trial, the testers congratulated one another. They ran the test a few more times, and their methods worked. They now plan to take their findings to the authorities, who can assess whether this type of drone delivery could accelerate humanitarian relief. Several other types and sizes of drones are already in use, including to deliver emergency rations to remote areas.

Speed is critical. The flood destroyed more than 35 bridges and damaged around 25 miles of roads, including sections of critical highways.

Nepal’s foreign minister, Swarnim Wagle, told Reuters that it more than $4 billion could be needed rebuild the destroyed infrastructure. To restore some connectivity, Nepal has requested portable bridges from other countries to assist with its emergency operations.

item.title: More Than 22,000 Ancient Artifacts Seized in Florida
item.description:
More than 22,000 ancient artifacts from around the world, some of which date back 5,000 years, were seized by officials in Florida in an effort to disrupt criminal networks involved in smuggling cultural property, the authorities said.

The items include vases, weapons, jewelry and mosaic picture frames, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency said in a statement on Friday. The agency said the seizure was among the largest of its Homeland Security Investigations unit.

The artifacts also include Egyptian statues and Byzantine glass vessels as well as ancient Greek and Roman coins, the statement said.

“The artifacts in this case that are determined to be genuine will be one of a kind, and H.S.I. wants to take every step necessary to ensure a civilization’s history is preserved for generations to come,” Mary Cook, a senior adviser in the unit’s Cultural Property, Art and Antiquities program, said in the statement.

Initial assessments indicate that some objects may have originated from civilizations from 1,000 to 5,000 years ago and come from sites in Europe, Africa and the eastern Mediterranean, according to ICE.

The authorities did not say where or when the recovery took place and did not provide details about any arrests or charges. ICE did not immediately respond to an inquiry on Sunday.

The agency noted that the identification of the artifacts would take time because “unlike narcotics, there is no field test for antiquities.”

The agency added that officials would work with experts from universities to help identify and authenticate the items. Those schools include the University of South Florida and the University of Pennsylvania.

ICE said it “targets criminal networks involved in the theft, smuggling and sale of artifacts,” such as those stolen from archaeological sites and museums.

“The trafficking of cultural property not only robs civilizations of their heritage, but also channels money into transnational criminal organizations, results in international financial crimes and, in some cases, even funds terrorist activities,” Micah McCombs, acting special agent in charge at Homeland Security Investigations in Tampa, said in the statement.

Officials said these types of investigations aim to preserve artifacts and return them to their countries of origin.

“The international demand for cultural property makes the theft a highly profitable crime, with relatively low risk compared to offenses such as narcotics smuggling,” ICE said.

item.title: Nepal Turns to Mass Burials, as Thousands Remain Missing from Floods
item.description:
Five days after an angry deluge tore through the mountain passes of Nepal, family members arriving after long journeys looked for something — anything — that could identify their loved ones amid the hundreds of mangled bodies.

In one hall in the downstream city of Bharatpur, men and women stared at a small television screen, watching a slide show of recovered remains in complete silence.

Next door, another government hall turned makeshift morgue housed the 270 sets of remains whose photos had been flashing on that screen. Nearly all remained unidentified.

Bharatpur, over 100 miles from where the floods first hit, had no capacity to preserve the corpses that washed up to its riverbanks, and could not keep them any longer. They were being transported to a forest for a mass burial before darkness took over the city.

At the burial spot, security forces in protective gear offloaded the bodies one by one onto stretchers, as cameras documented each step. Nearby, rows of metal numbered signs stuck into concrete-filled pots — the markers for each grave — awaited.

Only a fraction of the missing are turning up among the dead, underscoring a bleak reality: The death toll is likely to keep rising.

As of Sunday night local time, nearly 800 bodies had been found. More than 2,500 people were still missing, when the initial 72 hours after a disaster are usually seen as critical to a rescue operation.

The devastating flood swept through northern Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday after part of a glacier sheared off a mountain face, and its fall created such seismic force that officials initially believed it was an earthquake. The massive wall of water and mud it created swept up villagers, hydropower workers and hundreds of tourists and travelers from nearly three dozen countries on religious pilgrimages. Tens of thousands of people remain in need of relief, with entire towns wiped out, and roads, bridges and communication lines destroyed.

The bulk of the ongoing rescue effort has focused on the tunnels of several major hydropower projects in Rasuwa, which saw some of the earliest and fiercest damage in Nepal, and in Nuwakot, just downstream.

Through a night of rain, the army had tried to drill its way to tunnels buried under debris and mud. By Sunday afternoon, with support from Indian rescue teams, they had managed to find an opening to one tunnel, which they found brimming with water, according to Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, the army spokesman. A second tunnel has proved more difficult to locate an opening to, he said.

“The Nepali Army has been using thermal drones to search for signs of life,” he said. “But there have been no indications of survivors so far.”

The force of the deluge was such that nearly a dozen bodies were swept hundreds of miles away and found in India.

When the remains started washing up on the riverbanks of the Chitwan district, dozens of miles downstream from where the floods first hit, the officials were immediately overwhelmed.

Nepal is a deeply poor country, with limited infrastructure. The morgues in Chitwan have the capacity for storing just over three dozen bodies, Police Chief Rameshwor Poudel said.

With no good alternatives, district officials turned to the government hall in Bharatpur. Since it only had one air-conditioner, they tried to procure dry ice. They set up a help desk and a visitor hall. And they photographed the remains, so the loved ones who were beginning to trickle in could identify their missing.

But the bodies had been in water for so long. The monsoon heat did not help. And the freezers the foreign minister had appealed for from his international counterparts were not materializing immediately.

Only about a dozen bodies were identified and handed over to their families for burial. More remains kept coming.

“We’re still finding 15 to 20 new bodies every day," said Anil Thapa, a senior traffic cop helping at the makeshift morgue. “This will keep going on for months.”

On Saturday, the district authorities announced that they would begin burying the remains after a thorough process of documentation that includes taking photographs, recording distinguishing marks or clothing articles found on the corpses, and collecting DNA samples.

In a lush forest glade, a 10-minute drive away, they buried 93 bodies late Saturday, and another 100 the next day.

During the closing hours of the mass burial on Sunday evening, Biresh Kumar Sah, 17, reached the town’s makeshift morgue after an eight-hour bus ride.

He was studying in the Nepali capital when he first heard that the flood had hit his hometown, Siraha. His father, a math teacher, and his younger brother, who studied at the same school, were missing.

“The first day I tried to ignore it. I hid the information from everyone,” he said. “I wanted to still have hope.”

On the second day, he posted online that his father was missing.

“His colleague reached out and let me know he had seen my father and my brother being swept by the flood,” he said.

“I know they’re gone,” he added. “But I still have hope.”

His aunt, standing behind him, said the family would have to accept the emerging facts and prepare to hold final rites.

Biresh interjected, rolling his eyes.

“I don’t know these rites,” he said. “I feel wretched.”

Ramesh Dahal, 31, who had also looked at the photos on the screen, said he had reached Bharatpur after first checking all the hospitals in Kathmandu where the wounded had been taken.

He was looking for his 21-year-old nephew, Suman Dahal, a guide who had been leading a group of trekkers in Rasuwa.

Mr. Dahal said he had initially remained hopeful, after hearing reports that some people had fled to higher ground in the jungles as the floods descended.

Maybe they had felt the earthquake-like force of the falling glacier that had created the flood, and gone somewhere safe, he speculated. “Maybe they heard a siren from China,” he said.

But with each passing day, he said, he was coming to accept the reality.

“Now I feel there’s perhaps 0.1 percent chance to even to find his body,” he said.

Binod Ghimire contributed reporting from Kathmandu.

]]>

item.title: Expedia Faces Off With Cuban Families Over Land Seized Decades Ago
item.description:
Little did Mario Echevarria know, growing up, that the site of his father’s cattle and charcoal business on a cay north of Cuba would one day become a jewel in the Communist island’s tourism industry.

Now 87, stooped and gray-haired, Mr. Echevarria is seeking damages against Expedia Group, the travel booking giant, for failing to obtain his permission when reserving rooms in hotels built on Cayo Coco, land confiscated from his family in 1960.

Testifying in Miami federal court last week, he was asked who authorized the bookings.

“That was given to them by the dictatorship,” he said.

The civil trial is the second in the past 18 months against Expedia, whose lawyers argue the company believed it was acting legally. The claims stem from a section of a 1996 law that lets U.S. citizens — including Cubans who were not Americans at the time — accuse companies of having illegally “trafficked” in assets seized without compensation.

Expedia entered Cuba in 2017, after President Barack Obama issued new rules letting American hotel chains operate there.

The lawsuit is one in a surge by Cuban families making claims over confiscated assets, dating back to the beginning of the Cuban Revolution in 1959, and comes as President Trump intensifies a pressure campaign on the island.

These claims pit the historical demands of Cuban exiles against the interests of corporations that have tried to navigate the island’s market amid volatile U.S. policy. During his second term, Mr. Trump has oscillated between wanting to work with Cuba’s government and developing plans to overthrow it, all while expanding sanctions.

Mr. Trump took a hard-line stance toward Cuba in his first term, including by opening the door to the current lawsuits. He did that by ending a decades-long suspension of part of the 1996 law, the Helms-Burton Act, which Cuba calls an assault on its sovereignty. Since then, the law has been used to sue various businesses, including cruise lines, energy companies and mining operations.

Forty to 50 lawsuits have been filed in U.S. federal courts, legal experts note, with cases reaching the Supreme Court.

In 2025, a Miami federal jury awarded almost $30 million to Mr. Echevarria in damages related to three hotels on Cayo Coco where Expedia and its affiliate sites operated.

A judge set aside the jury verdict, saying Expedia couldn’t be held liable for its subsidiaries. The case is under appeal. Expedia lawyers declined to comment.

The latest trial against Expedia involves bookings at four other hotels on Cayo Coco as well as the San Carlos Hotel in Cienfuegos, on Cuba’s south coast. All had been operated by a Spanish hotel chain, Meliá, which quit Cuba this summer. Although the chain did not cite U.S. sanctions as a factor, experts said they most likely contributed to the decision.

The families seek damages calculated to the market value of the properties, collectively estimated at $82 million.

Maricela Mata, 66, told the jury how she and her brother were born in the San Carlos Hotel, which her family owned and lived in. In 1981, she said, “the Communists told us we had to leave because the hotel was going to be renovated.” The family was never allowed back.

Esther Echevarria, 88, Mario’s sister-in-law, told the jury that when her family moved to Cayo Coco as a girl (her father rented property from the Echevarrias), the cay was all inhospitable mangroves, infested with mosquitoes and sandflies. “There was nothing, nothing there at all, just the charcoal makers,” she said.

After the authorities took the land, she said, her father resorted to selling water and bread nearby. It wasn’t until the 1990s that the government began developing the land for tourism.

Expedia’s lawyers argued they “did not knowingly and intentionally traffic” in the property, as they were unaware the hotels were on confiscated land.

On the stand, a former Expedia manager, Veronica Cassano, said her superiors never instructed her about the Helms-Burton law.

She described meetings with high-level Cuban officials, and said she did not have any conversations with Expedia about Cayo Coco’s historical ownership.

Santosh Aravind, a lawyer for Expedia, told the court that such meetings were a necessary and legitimate part of setting up operations in Cuba, where the state owns all hotels. Furthermore, this was done with the full knowledge and approval of the U.S. Treasury Department, he said, noting that one meeting with a senior Cuban official took place at top U.S. diplomat’s residence.

The plaintiffs’ lawyers accused Expedia of playing fast and loose with U.S. rules, which permit travel to Cuba only under 12 authorized categories, none of which are resort tourism. They described Cayo Coco as a stretch of pristine beaches, hundreds of miles from Havana and home to a dozen modern hotels.

“There’s not a church, not a school, not a stadium, no housing for Cubans, and only one medical clinic for foreigners,” said one of the plaintiffs’ lawyers, Jorge Mestre. “It’s fun in the sun, it’s bars and beach.”

Ordinary Cubans who do not work in the hotel sector, they added, are forbidden entry to the cay.

item.title: U.A.E. to Review Egyptian Bank as Part of U.S. Sanctions on Iran
item.description:
The central bank of the United Arab Emirates announced on Saturday that it would conduct a “special and urgent examination” of an Egyptian bank operating in the country, the latest fallout from the Treasury Department’s renewed push to isolate Iran.

The U.S. Treasury Department said last week that the Egyptian bank, the state-owned Banque Misr, was helping Iran evade sanctions, drawing fresh attention to the Emirates’ role as a hub for trade with Iran.

The department proposed a rule that would prevent the bank’s Emirati branches from doing business with American financial institutions. It also called the bank “a critical node for the Iranian regime’s access to U.S. dollars.” It estimated that between January 2024 and June 2026, the bank’s Emirati branches had processed about $1.8 billion in transactions “that are potentially part of Iranian shadow banking networks,” enabling the Islamic republic to evade U.S. sanctions.

“Treasury promised to sever every economic lifeline Tehran has left and finally end the threat of the Iranian regime,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the statement on Friday. Last week, he announced another round of economic warfare against Iran in the form of sanctions against dozens of entities, individuals and vessels.

Banque Misr said it was treating the allegations with “utmost seriousness and attention” and planned to cooperate with the Treasury Department.

The bank adheres to “all applicable laws, regulations, instructions and supervisory controls,” it said in a statement. The suggested regulatory action would not affect Banque Misr branches in Egypt or other countries aside from the Emirates, the bank added.

The U.S. Treasury Department also imposed sanctions on the manager of an Emirati branch of Bank Melli, Iran’s largest lender, and a Hong Kong-based company that it said had helped launder funds for an Iranian exchange house that is under U.S. sanctions.

The Emirates, located just 50 miles from Iran across the Persian Gulf, has nurtured close economic and cultural ties with Iran for decades despite political tensions between the two countries.

Analysts said that trade through Dubai, the Emirates’ largest city, had long been essential to Iranian efforts to evade sanctions, eliciting complaints and pressure from the American authorities.

The Treasury Department said that Banque Misr had facilitated transactions for “front companies” based in the Emirates, some of which it said were involved in the flow of money to Iran’s defense ministry and Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

The Emirati central bank said it was “studying the available options regarding the status of the bank” in case the Treasury Department decided to move forward with its proposed action.

Emirati officials say that they crack down on any sanctions violations when they find them. This month, the government said it was halting all trade and financial transactions with Iran. The announcement came one day before the Trump administration said it was starting its renewed economic campaign against Iran.

item.title: Long Lines for Gas in Iran Show War and U.S. Blockade Squeezing Supply
item.description:
Lines of cars waiting to fill up at Iran’s gas stations, even in the middle of the night, have become a common sight in recent weeks, Iranians said in interviews, as war and a U.S. blockade have strained fuel supplies.

The Iranian government is struggling with how to respond and is wary of reducing expensive subsidies, a move that would raise fuel prices and that has prompted large-scale protests in the past.

Though Iran is rich in crude oil, its refining capacity has long been insufficient to meet the country’s gasoline demand, officials and experts say. The shortfall — just over a tenth of the gasoline consumed per day, according to government figures — is usually made up by imports. Now those have been all but cut off by the continuing U.S. naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports.

Domestic production of gasoline has also decreased since the U.S.-Israeli war, officials say, as strikes have damaged Iranian refineries and limited their capacity.

Iranians reached in several cities, including Tehran, Isfahan and Bandar Abbas, said they had seen long lines at gas stations in recent days.

“Even when you pass through the streets around midnight, like 2 or 3 in the morning, you will see that there is a huge line of cars standing and waiting in line,” said Reyhaneh, 30, an unemployed teacher in the city of Mashhad. Like others reached in Iran, she asked that her last name not be used for fear of retribution.

The prospect of increased fuel prices is compounding difficulties for Iranians, as the war enters its seventh month with no clear resolution in sight. Iranians are already facing 80 percent inflation over this time last year, the central bank has said, as well as widespread job losses caused, in part, by the war and a government-imposed internet shutdown.

The U.S. blockade has been aimed in part at pressuring Tehran to loosen its grip on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping waterway in the Persian Gulf that Iranian forces effectively closed early in the war. The bottleneck has caused an increase in the price of fuel globally, including in the United States.

On Monday, the U.S. government announced additional sanctions on Iran and Iran-linked entities, hoping the measures would force the Islamic republic to make concessions.

The situation has left the Iranian government with few options. In 2019, a sharp increase in gasoline prices set off mass protests that the authorities put down with violence.

Economic discontent also caused nationwide demonstrations early this year. Officials are keenly aware that raising gas prices now could set off a new round of protests.

Iran’s Parliament speaker and lead negotiator with Washington, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said this month that though gasoline consumption had to be reduced, raising prices was a mistake. Iran’s “enemy” plans to exploit the issue to create unrest, he claimed, while not specifying what the government should do instead.

Amirhossein Khaleghi, an economist in Iran, said, “When the government lacks sufficient legitimacy and resources, and especially in the middle of a war, the question is how we can continue with the current situation when we no longer have the resources to sustain it.”

Iranian officials have acknowledged some of the scale of the crisis and the effects of U.S. pressure but have still sought to project defiance.

“We are facing war,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said in an interview with Iranian state television on Friday. “The enemy has targeted our oil and gas resources, and our production has fallen. We are standing firm in the war, but we have to help increase the country’s resilience.”

Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, issued a statement on Friday acknowledging “economic and livelihood challenges” while warning officials not to publicize or highlight government weaknesses, so as to avoid benefiting Iran’s enemies.

The gasoline issue is just one of several arenas in which the government has struggled to provide basic infrastructure and align supply with demand. Iran’s electricity usage also exceeds what its infrastructure can deliver.

In his interview, Mr. Pezeshkian urged Iranians to reduce their consumption and said he leaves his office lights off and uses a fan instead of air-conditioning.

In Iran, the government has long provided cheap energy to help make life somewhat manageable even as prices for other goods skyrocket.

The government subsidizes gasoline at different tiers based on consumption, with some gas offered at less than one cent per liter at current exchange rates. There are quotas on how much can be bought at each price, and those quotas have been curtailed in recent weeks.

So far the government has appeared resistant to raising fuel prices. But while Mr. Pezeshkian has pledged that the price of gas at the cheapest tier of quotas will not increase, he said those consuming beyond a set amount could pay as much as double.

“If we raise the gasoline price recklessly, we will create problems for people,” Mr. Pezeshkian said, while lamenting that the government had been subsidizing fuel so deeply.

The looming crisis, though exacerbated by recent events, is the culmination of many longstanding problems.

Because fuel prices in Iran are so much lower than in neighboring countries, some of the subsidized gasoline is smuggled abroad for profit, officials and experts have said. The government has appeared unwilling or unable to stop the trade.

And even in large cities, public transit is inadequate to meet people’s needs, forcing them to rely on their own cars and taxis to get around.

Until that confluence of problems is addressed, said Reza Gheibi, an economic analyst in London, changes like restructuring the quotas “would, at best, change the way the shortage is distributed — not the shortage itself.”

The recent cuts to quotas for fuel have forced many Iranians to buy unsubsidized fuel, and they often must line up for hours as gas stations offer fewer of those pumps.

Soheil, an engineer in Isfahan, said that his city had relatively ample gasoline availability. And yet, he added, “even here, the queues at gas stations are getting longer and longer.”

item.title: Far Right Is Poised to Win in a German State, but Fight Over Power Won’t End There
item.description:
Government leaders across Germany are publicly and privately exploring ways to curb the power of the far-right Alternative for Germany party, or AfD, if it wins control of a state government in elections on Sept. 6.

The officials’ efforts, detailed in interviews and in statements by top officials, include attempts to throttle the routine sharing of certain classified information with state-level intelligence services should the AfD win control of them. They also involve less onerous measures aimed at policy matters. The planning is driven partly out of fear that AfD officials could pass national secrets to Russia, to which the party maintains close ties.

The AfD is poised to win the most votes in Sept. 6 elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt in Germany’s east. If it secures enough seats to form a governing coalition by itself, it will become the first far-right party since World War II to hold power in Germany.

Governing a state would typically grant a party access to national secrets, including about intelligence and security.

Many officials seeking to curb the AfD’s power see it as a threat to German democracy and national security, and say their plans are necessary to safeguard the country. Protection of democracy is a particularly sensitive issue in Germany, which after World War II designed its institutions to prevent extreme parties like the Nazis from ever returning to power.

The AfD’s rival parties consider it extreme. No other major party in Germany will work with it to form a government at the state or national level, a collusion that is known in Germany as “the firewall” and that the AfD has long assailed.

Boris Pistorius, Germany’s defense minister, told the tabloid news outlet Bild this summer that he would not pass classified information to an AfD government. He cited the AfD’s closeness to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, whom party leaders have praised.

“Their affinity for Putin is impossible to overlook,” Mr. Pistorius said. “To seriously believe that we should carelessly let this information fall into the wrong hands, I think it’s obvious that must not happen.”

In the eyes of the AfD and its supporters, those efforts are an attempt to trample the will of voters and thwart its policy agenda, which includes deporting migrants and banning gay Pride flags in schools.

“It’s not democratic, not political and not proper — it’s just kind of dirty,” Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s candidate for governor in Saxony-Anhalt, said in an interview on the Austrian populist channel ServusTV.

AfD officials in Saxony-Anhalt did not respond to repeated emailed requests for comment on the efforts to curb the party’s power should it win.

In many cases, the planning to try to curb the AfD is happening secretly, in fear that discussions will be leaked to the press and feed the party’s narrative that the German federal government is obstructing voters’ will.

Interior ministers in other states have circulated ideas for restricting the power of an AfD government should it take shape, including by denying its officials access to certain information with security implications, according to Georg Maier, the interior minister of the state of Thuringia in central Germany.

“I believe it’s a real problem, and that it’s a threat to national security if it happens,” he said in an interview.

Mr. Maier, a sharp critic of the AfD, declined to publicly detail the steps interior ministers were contemplating.

Federal intelligence services have labeled the AfD as suspected of being right-wing extremist. It also maintains connections to Russia, an increasingly hostile adversary. Elected officials from the AfD have set off a political furor by seeking to reveal national security secrets, some of which relate to Germany’s support for Ukraine, that could benefit Russian military planning. German officials have accused Russia of sabotage, cyberattacks and other efforts to undermine German social cohesion.

The AfD is leading the polls in two states, Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, that will vote next month. Both lie in the former East Germany, an AfD stronghold, where party leaders have harnessed social media and local organizing to appeal to voters frustrated by economic stagnation, immigration and cultural change.

The AfD appears close to an outright majority of seats in Saxony-Anhalt. That would allow it to form a government without the help of any other party, bypassing the firewall. Federal intelligence classifies the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt as confirmed extremist. Its potential ascent has some officials contemplating extreme steps under German law.

The country’s Constitution was written by survivors of the Nazi era after the war. To prevent extremist forces from taking power again, it allows the federal government to take over state police forces if the country’s “free democratic order” is in danger.

Sven Hüber, a high-ranking police union official with no public party affiliation, compared a possible AfD takeover in Saxony-Anhalt to the ascent of the Nazi party in the 1930s. In a letter in a police union newsletter, he reassured officers that the union would help members who refused to carry out illegal orders from “undemocratic” ministers.

AfD allies struck back. Mr. Hüber was forced to resign from the union this week after a far-right news platform published a report accusing him of acts of violence during his time as an East German border guard in the 1980s. In a statement, Mr. Hüber called the accusations “defamatory and slanderous” and said he had taken legal action in response.

Government officials elsewhere are publicly contemplating less drastic measures to respond to an AfD win.

A group of ministers from other German states is considering a change that would stop a potential AfD state government from blocking some educational funding. The money requires unanimous approval by representatives from each state.

Saxony-Anhalt’s governing coalition also passed a law this spring meant to stop any one party from vetoing judicial appointments or blocking the appointment of a governor it does not like.

The law allows parties that do not finish first in an election to band together to nominate a head of the legislature. Previously, only the first-place party could nominate a candidate for the state legislature to approve. The change could allow mainstream parties this fall to elect their own choice to run the state if the AfD wins but fails to secure a majority.

State leaders in Saxony-Anhalt, including the center-right governor, Sven Schulze, took pains to say it was not targeting a single party. In an interview, Mr. Schulze said the democratic way to stop the AfD was at the ballot box.

Changing a range of rules to single out the AfD and block it from power “would be a capitulation, and I won’t go along with that,” he said.

Recently, Mr. Schulze adopted another tactic in a bid to win elections: He embraced parts of the AfD’s message.

Mr. Schulze echoed a longtime AfD call to remove terrorism suspects from Germany even if they are citizens, after a German-born man killed a woman and injured 29 people near a Berlin Pride event last month. The attacker had unsuccessfully tried to join the Islamic State terrorist group. “We simply can’t allow people to live here who don’t accept our culture,” Mr. Schulze said.

]]>

item.title: Google Maps Changes Lake Ontario to Lake America
item.description:
Google has updated its Maps application, labeling Lake Ontario as Lake America for users in the United States, following an executive order signed by President Trump last week amid an escalating trade war with Canada.

The decision of the tech giant reflects what it did when Mr. Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America last year.

The change has started to be rolled out, Google said in a blog post, adding that it was following its practice of using the name given by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System.

“People using Maps in the U.S. will see “Lake America,” those in Canada will continue to see “Lake Ontario,” and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names,” Google said in its statement.

Mr. Trump’s decision to rename the lake on Thursday was met with derision and shrugs in Canada and across the United States, and sparked a series of online memes and late-night jokes.

He leaned into his decision, posting an A.I.-generated video depicting ducks armed with semiautomatic weapons and donning his signature quiff, shooting the guns and seemingly protecting a lake under a sign that read “Lake America.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada walked away from fraught U.S. trade talks on Aug. 21, over what he called a “bad deal” that would harm Canada’s economy and sovereignty. He has since responded to the renaming of the lake with a statement about its history, noting that Ontario is a historical Indigenous name for the lake that predates the creation of Canada and the United States.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” Mr. Carney said in his post on Thursday. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always.”

Premier Doug Ford of Ontario on Saturday unveiled a large sign by the lake in Winona, Ontario, that read “Lake Ontario Now and Always” and repeated the same in French, as is standard in Canada: “Lac Ontario Aujourd’hui et pour toujours.”

“It was like something out of ‘Saturday Night Live’ when he signed a document saying change it to Lake America,” Mr. Ford said on “This Week With George Stephanopoulos,” broadcast on Sunday. “No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario. It’s just so disappointing.”

The collapse of the trade talks earlier this month triggered new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods, and was countered by Canadian tariffs on American goods expected to take effect Sept. 8.

It has also unleashed a war of words, with Mr. Trump reviving his longstanding comments about Canada becoming the 51st state, and calling Mr. Carney and the Canadian leadership “nasty.”

Canadians have rallied behind Mr. Carney, but are bracing for the economic impact of a protracted dispute with their neighbor and biggest trading ally.

item.title: Hunt Underway After Deadly Shooting at Swiss Rave
item.description:
The Swiss police are looking for one or more people who killed one woman and wounded five others at a rave in Switzerland on Sunday.

The shooting happened during a dance party at a horseracing track in Aarau, in the country’s north. A number of shots were fired, the police said, but on Sunday afternoon it was still unclear how many perpetrators and how many guns were involved.

A police spokesman said that they were searching the entire country but that the risk for people in the area was believed to be low since they thought the perpetrator or perpetrators had fled.

The shooting happened early Sunday as the rave was winding down, the spokesman said.

A 22-year-old woman died at the scene, and four men and a woman, aged 24 to 27, were wounded, according to the police. All six victims were Swiss citizens.

The army also dispatched a special forces unit to the scene and a helicopter to help in the manhunt.

Switzerland, which has a universal army draft, allows most men who have undergone basic training to keep their army weapons at home to help in domestic defense. However, most are not allowed to keep ammunition at home.

The shooting came nine months after a disaster in Crans-Montana, in the country’s south, left 41 people dead and dozens catastrophically burned when a fire erupted at a bar on New Year’s Eve.

On Sunday morning, the organizers of the rave released a statement on Instagram saying they were thinking of the victims, their friends and families.

“The cowardly attack on the guests at the Aarau rave has broken our hearts,” they wrote. “A rave should always be a place of joy and love.”

item.title: Ferry Carrying Hundreds of Passengers Capsizes Off Coast of Cyprus
item.description:
A passenger ferry carrying 267 people capsized off the northern coast of Cyprus on Sunday, leaving several people dead and prompting a search and rescue effort for the remaining passengers.

At least seven people died and 237 were rescued, said Unal Ustel, the prime minister of the part of northern Cyprus that has declared itself an independent Turkish republic. Some 23 others were unaccounted for, he added. “Our top priority right now is to reach the 23 missing individuals as soon as possible,” he said.

The ferry had departed the Cypriot port of Kyrenia (known as Girne in Turkish) for Tasucu, in southern Turkey. Turkey’s Interior Ministry said it was carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members when it began taking on water about four miles from Kyrenia.

Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz of Turkey described the vessel as a “catamaran-type” boat. “I extend my condolences to the passengers on board, the crew and our nation,” he said on social media.

The interior ministry said in a statement that Turkish and northern Cypriot forces had started an expansive search-and-rescue effort involving helicopters and naval units.

“We are deeply saddened,” said Unal Ustel, the prime minister of northern Cyprus, according to his office’s Facebook page. “There has been loss of life, and there are injured people.”

No information was immediately available about the nationalities of those aboard the ship. Passengers on such routes are predominantly residents of northern Cyprus, many of whom carry Turkish or Cypriot passports, and Turks from mainland Turkey.

In an interview with Anadolu, Turkey’s state-run news agency, Mr. Ustel said the ferry’s departure had been delayed by a day because of bad weather. “It was hit by a first wave at sea, and while the captain was trying to recover, the vessel began taking on water after a second wave hit,” he told the outlet.

The Turkish military occupied territory in northern Cyprus in 1974 amid violence between the ethnic Greek and Turkish populations on the Mediterranean island. In 1983, northern Cyprus declared itself an independent Turkish republic, a move that is not recognized by any country except Turkey.
